title: Seventh Copy — Xerox Punk Manifesto
description: A photocopy-degraded punk flyer template channeling ransom-note typography and zine xerox texture. Rotated type blocks, tape-mark corners, and halftone bleed set it apart from clean, geometric digital brutalism.
philosophy: This template exists as an act of refusal. It rejects the smoothness of modern slide design — no gradients, no shadows, no rounded forgiveness — because some ideas should feel dangerous and immediate, not committee-approved. It is built for speakers who want their opener to hit like a flyer stapled to a wet telephone pole at 2 AM. Precision is the enemy here; every misalignment is load-bearing.
goodFor: Hackathon kickoff sessions with a counter-culture or anti-corporate tone
Underground event, unconference, or manifesto-style talks
3–6 slide provocations and lightning talks where shock is the point
Zine launches, activist campaigns, or DIY cultural events
avoidFor: Investor pitch decks or board-level financial reviews
Luxury, wellness, or premium brand presentations
Academic thesis defenses requiring institutional credibility
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The slide should feel like a seventh-generation photocopy — information degraded to raw urgency. Halftone grain bleeds across the entire field; tape-mark artifacts anchor the corners as though the whole thing was stapled to a wet wall at midnight. The composition is asymmetric and confrontational, the title crashing in from the left on a canted axis while the subtitle counter-angles below a torn-rule divide. No smoothness, no symmetry, no digital forgiveness — every misalignment is intentional, every texture a declaration.

examples.layoutNotes: The title slide operates on a 12-column grid that its own elements deliberately violate. The primary title block anchors left-of-center, rotated a few degrees counter-clockwise and cropped hard at the left bleed edge. A subtitle or secondary text block occupies the lower-right zone, counter-rotated, separated from the title by a thick hand-torn horizontal rule. Tape-mark rectangles occupy all four corners; a stamped deck identifier sits bottom-left flush to the margin with no header band — the full surface is treated as active, raw terrain.

examples.promptCore: The slide should feel like a xeroxed flyer pulled from the bottom of a wet stack — grain-heavy, slightly overexposed, with type that refuses to stay in its lane. Composition is aggressively off-balance: one blunt assertion commands most of the surface while smaller text fragments orbit it like torn caption strips or cut-and-paste ransom notes. The mood is urgent, hand-assembled, and confrontational; suppress any sense of alignment comfort, gradient softness, or modular cleanliness. Nothing should look committee-approved or safe.
